knowledgeAnswers.rationale: Ground-based methods keep the worker's feet on a stable surface and reduce the need for height. They still carry hazards, so the option claiming all risk is removed is wrong.
A defective section is removed from service, tagged and reported. Using it on calm days or taping the joint is not an acceptable control.

A line within reach with clearance that cannot be checked means the pole stays down and the job is referred. Working quickly or asking the customer to switch off power is not a substitute for a checked clearance.
A held exclusion zone with barriers or a supervisor is the control. Verbal warnings and signs alone do not keep the drop zone clear.
Wash water and detergent are kept out of stormwater as the job plan requires. The plan must control the runoff.

practicalCriteria: Before assembly, the learner surveys the full reach for overhead lines and records the result.
The learner inspects every pole section and joint, and removes any defective part from service with a tag.
The learner sets a wind threshold and an exclusion zone in the job plan before starting.
The learner keeps runoff out of stormwater and has the safety data sheet for the product on site.
The learner stops and lowers the pole when a line, a footing change or a person enters the zone.
passRule: Knowledge checks: 80% correct (4 of 5). Practical sign-off is assessed separately by an assessor using the practical criteria. A knowledge pass does not verify pole competence.
evidenceRequired: Equipment inspection record with defects found and action taken
Overhead line survey record with the clearance decision
Job plan showing wind threshold, exclusion zone and runoff control
Safety data sheet reference for the product used
stopWorkCriteria: An overhead line is within reach and clearance cannot be checked.
A pole section is cracked, bent or has a damaged seal and is still used.
Wind exceeds the job plan threshold or the footing shifts.
Wash water is discharged to stormwater without a plan.
